name: Chromatic Aberration
basis: why: dispersion makes a lens land red, green and blue apart; how: channels read at radially scaled positions

lumenary.blurb: A lens cannot bend every colour by the same amount. Red, green and blue land in slightly different places, and the edges split into colour.

facts.bestOn: High contrast edges, such as signs, branches and city lights

why: Glass bends each colour of light by a slightly different amount, a property called dispersion, so a lens cannot bring red, green and blue into exactly the same place. The channels land a little apart, and edges split into colour. This treatment does what the lens does: it reads red, green and blue from slightly different places, and the difference grows toward the edges of the picture.
how: In radial mode keep the green channel where it is, read red from a point further out and blue from a point further in.

Scale the shift by half the amount times one minus the edge strength plus 2.2 times the edge strength times the squared distance from the centre, so with full edge strength it grows with the square of distance.
In sideways mode shift red and blue by a fixed amount along one direction, like a prism.
In full spectrum mode take seven samples along the line, with red weighted from one end, blue from the other and green from the middle, each normalised to add to 1.
Add an optional soft glow from a tenth-scale copy screened on.
history: Isaac Newton showed in 1666 that a prism splits white light into colours, and he built the first reflecting telescope in 1668 partly to avoid the coloured fringes of lenses. Chester Moore Hall and John Dollond developed achromatic lenses, which combine two glasses to cancel much of the fringing, in the eighteenth century. Today it is a flaw that photographers correct, and an effect designers add on purpose.
uses: Photo realism for CGI and game scenes
terms: Different colours bending by different amounts when light passes through glass.
Colour fringes caused by different magnification of each colour.
A lens made from two kinds of glass to bring two colours to the same focus.
paragraphs: A glass lens bends each colour of light by a slightly different amount, a property called dispersion. The result is lateral chromatic aberration: the red, green and blue images are enlarged by slightly different factors, so they separate more the farther they are from the centre of the picture. The program does what the lens does. In the radial mode the green channel stays where it is, the red channel is read from a point u further out, and the blue from a point u further in. The shift has the size A/2 × [(1 − e) + 2.2 e ρ²], where ρ is the distance from the centre divided by the half-diagonal and e the strongest-at-the-edges slider, so with e = 1 it grows with the square of the distance.

The sideways mode shifts red and blue by a fixed amount along one direction (the angle slider), like a prism, optionally growing toward the edges. The full-spectrum mode takes seven samples along the line from −u to +u. Red takes its weight from the + end, blue from the − end and green from the middle, and each channel’s weights are normalised to add up to 1, so a flat colour comes through unchanged and an edge is smeared into a rainbow. A soft glow (a tenth-scale copy, screened on) is optional.

equations.note: Radial shift: A is the amount in pixels, e the edge slider, c the centre and R the half-diagonal.

equations.tex: R'(\mathbf x)=R(\mathbf x+\mathbf u),\qquad G'(\mathbf x)=G(\mathbf x),\qquad B'(\mathbf x)=B(\mathbf x-\mathbf u)
equations.note: The three channels are sampled at different places (bilinear interpolation).

equations.tex: C'_c(\mathbf x)=\sum_{k=0}^{6} w_c(k)\;C_c\!\Big(\mathbf x+\mathbf u\,\big(\tfrac{k}{3}-1\big)\Big),\qquad w_c\propto\max\big(0,\ 1-\gamma_c\lvert t_k-t_c\rvert\big)
equations.note: Full-spectrum mode: t_k = k/6; t_c = 1, ½, 0 and γ_c = 1.7, 2.3, 1.7 for red, green and blue; weights add up to 1.

presets.text: Strong radial fringing with edges maxed looks like a cheap lens.
Sideways mode with a diagonal angle looks like a glitch.
Full spectrum smears edges into a rainbow.
